research_text:
# Research brief

## 1. API and reported value

`javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory` converts between secret-key objects and transparent key specifications; it operates on symmetric keys. Its static `getInstance` methods take an **algorithm name** and optionally a provider. The reported value, `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1`, refers to that algorithm argument—not to the password, salt, iteration count, or derived key. Oracle documents standard names of the form `PBKDF2With<prf>`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html#secretkeyfactory-algorithms

The stated `UnsafeAlgorithm` result is a **rule-policy mismatch**: the reported name is absent from the CrySL allowlist. It is not, by itself, a Java API error. Oracle’s JDK 8 SunJCE documentation lists `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1` as supported. Standard Java algorithm names are documented as case-insensitive; the rule file alone does not establish whether the detector normalizes names. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl))

## 2. Documented usage and remediation

Oracle says to consult the selected provider’s documentation for supported key specifications. `generateSecret` accepts a `KeySpec`; `PBEKeySpec` can contain a password, salt, iteration count, and requested derived-key length. It provides `clearPassword()` for its internal password copy, and callers are responsible for clearing password copies returned by `getPassword()`. An unavailable algorithm results in `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/spec/PBEKeySpec.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html

For the **rule’s policy**, its allowed choices include `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` and other SHA-2 variants, plus the specified PBE-with-HMAC-and-AES names. The rule does not constrain the password, salt, iteration count, or key length. Oracle’s class documentation does **not** prescribe a specific remediation for this finding or declare every use of `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA1` invalid. RFC 8018 recommends PBKDF2 for new applications and describes salt and iteration count as separate parameters; selecting an allowed name alone therefore does not establish that a complete configuration is appropriate. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl))

Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8018

## 3. Compatibility and migration

- **Existing data and wire formats:** Changing the PBKDF2 PRF changes a derivation input and must not be assumed to reproduce existing derived keys. RFC 8018 defines PBKDF2 parameters including salt, iteration count, optional key length, and PRF; in its ASN.1 format an omitted PRF defaults to HMAC-SHA-1. For PBE decryption, Oracle says the parameters used for encryption must also be used for decryption. The API documentation does not specify an automatic migration of application data or wire formats. ([rfc-editor.org](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8018))
- **Documented migration consideration:** For password verifiers, NIST recommends storing a reference to the password-hashing scheme and cost factor to allow migration to new algorithms and work factors. This is password-verifier guidance, not a general migration procedure for encrypted files or protocols. ([pages.nist.gov](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html))
- **Platform support:** Oracle’s JDK 8 SunJCE list includes all four rule-allowed PBKDF2 SHA-2 names. Java SE 26 requires implementations to support `PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256` and the two SHA-256 PBE/AES names listed in its class documentation; other choices require implementation/provider documentation. This does not establish availability on every older JDK, Android release, or third-party provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/SunProviders.html))

Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html  
https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/SunProviders.html  
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/crypto/SecretKeyFactory.html

## 4. Exact CrySL rule

The supplied rule file declares `SPEC javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory`. Its matching event clauses are, verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl))

```text
	g1: getInstance(algorithm);
	g2: getInstance(algorithm, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	gS: key = generateSecret(keySpec);
	tK: key = translateKey(otherKey);
	Gen := gS | tK;
```

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl

The file declares `algorithm` as `String`, `keySpec` as `KeySpec`, and `key` and `otherKey` as `SecretKey`. The event clauses specify **one- and two-argument** `getInstance` forms and one-argument forms for the other two methods; `_` places no explicit value constraint on the second `getInstance` argument. The file specifies `Get, Gen`, constrains `algorithm` to the explicit 12-name allowlist in the question, requires `speccedKey[keySpec, _]`, and ensures `generatedKey[key, algorithm]`. One allowlist entry, `PBEWithHmacSHA384AndAES_128`, appears twice. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SecretKeyFactory.crysl))

**A shared method name alone is not what this rule declares:** its `SPEC` names `javax.crypto.SecretKeyFactory` and its events include argument lists. The file itself does not describe the detector’s resolution of unrelated same-named methods, subclasses, aliases, or unresolved calls. Consequently, whether a particular detector implementation could nevertheless report such a call remains **unresolved from this source alone**.

The URL points to a mutable `master` branch. The supplied SHA-256 was not independently verified against the retrieved file, so its identity with the rule version that produced the finding remains unresolved.
